items.title: Adam Smith warned against corporate collusion
items.claim: Adam Smith is often invoked as a free-market champion. What did he actually say about businessmen meeting together?

options.text: That free assembly among capitalists is the engine of innovation
That 'People of the same trade seldom meet together... but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices.'
That competition is a myth used by economists
Nothing — he never discussed business behaviour

items.reveal:
The quote is from The Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Chapter X. Smith was deeply suspicious of merchant power and joint-stock companies. He criticised the East India Company at length and warned that 'the proposal of any new law or regulation of commerce which comes from this order ought always to be listened to with great precaution.'

The 'invisible hand' appears only three times in his works, with a meaning closer to 'unintended consequences of self-interested behaviour, when channelled by competition' than 'markets always good'.
items.why: Smith is invoked rhetorically by people who haven't read him. The actual Wealth of Nations is alert to monopoly, collusion and the political power of capital — closer to a regulatory liberal than a libertarian.

items.title: Automatic stabilisers work without political decisions
items.claim: Unemployment benefits rise automatically in downturns; tax receipts fall as incomes drop. These automatic stabilisers do which of the following?

options.text: Smooth output and incomes without requiring discretionary decisions, providing counter-cyclical support faster than discretionary stimulus; the IMF estimates they typically absorb 20-50% of GDP shocks in advanced economies

items.reveal:
OECD analysis: stronger automatic stabilisers (more generous unemployment insurance, progressive taxation) reduce output volatility by ~25%. UK's automatic stabilisers are relatively weaker than the European average.

Discretionary fiscal policy (stimulus packages) is slower (legislation lag, implementation lag) and politically contested. Robert Hall and others have argued for stronger automatic mechanisms as a complement to monetary policy.
items.why: Policy that operates automatically removes one source of delay and politicisation. The design of stabilisers shapes how recessions transmit through the economy.

items.title: The Phillips curve broke down spectacularly in the 1970s
items.claim: Bill Phillips's 1958 paper documented an inverse relationship between UK unemployment and wage inflation. What happened in the 1970s?

options.text: The relationship held perfectly, vindicating Keynesian demand management
The US and UK experienced 'stagflation' — high inflation AND high unemployment simultaneously, which the simple Phillips curve said was impossible
The relationship inverted entirely; lower unemployment led to deflation
Statistical data became unreliable, so no test was possible

items.reveal:
The 1970s combined oil shocks (1973, 1979), wage-price spirals and weak productivity growth. US inflation reached 13.5% in 1980; unemployment was 7.5%. Both up, together.

Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps had argued in the late 1960s that the long-run Phillips curve was vertical at the 'natural rate' of unemployment — once expectations adjusted, only the natural rate was stable. The 1970s vindicated them and supplied the intellectual ammunition for monetarism, Volcker and Thatcher.

Modern expectations-augmented Phillips curves are still used but are far less crisp than the original.
items.why: The Phillips curve example is the cleanest case of a model that worked, then didn't. It's also why mid-20th-century Keynesianism gave way to monetarism, with consequences that still shape macro policy.
